{{Short description|Operator equation in the style of Fredholm theory}}
{{distinguish|Product integral}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Volterra integral equations''' are a special type of [[integral equation]]s, named after [[Vito Volterra]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Polyanin|first=Andrei D.|title=Handbook of Integral Equations|last2=Manzhirov|first2=Alexander V.|publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC|year=2008|isbn=978-1584885078|edition=2nd|location=Boca Raton, FL}}</ref> They are divided into two groups referred to as the first and the second kind.

A linear Volterra equation of the first kind is

:<math> f(t) = \int_a^t K(t,s)\,x(s)\,ds</math>

where <math> f(t) </math> is a given function and <math> x(t) </math> is to be determined.  A linear Volterra equation of the second kind is

:<math> x(t) = f(t) + \int_a^t K(t,s)x(s)\,ds. </math>

In [[operator theory]], and in [[Fredholm theory]], the corresponding operators are called [[Volterra operator]]s.  A useful method to solve such equations, the [[Adomian decomposition method]], is due to [[George Adomian]].

A linear Volterra integral equation is a [[convolution]] equation if

:<math> x(t) = f(t) + \int_{t_0}^t K(t-s)x(s)\,ds. </math>

The function <math> K </math> in the integral is called the [[Integral transform|kernel]]. Such equations can be analyzed and solved by means of [[Laplace transform]] techniques.

For a weakly singular kernel of the form <math>K(t,s) = (t^2-s^2)^{-\alpha}</math> with <math>0<\alpha<1</math>, Volterra integral equation of the first kind can conveniently be transformed into a classical Abel integral equation. 

The Volterra integral equations were introduced by Vito Volterra and then studied by [[Traian Lalescu]] in his 1908 thesis, ''Sur les équations de Volterra'', written under the direction of [[Charles Émile Picard|Émile Picard]].   In 1911, Lalescu wrote the first book ever on integral equations.

Volterra integral equations find application in [[demography]] as [[Lotka's integral equation]],<ref>{{cite book |first=Hisashi |last=Inaba |chapter=The Stable Population Model |title=Age-Structured Population Dynamics in Demography and Epidemiology |pages=1–74 |location=Singapore |publisher=Springer |year=2017 |isbn=978-981-10-0187-1 |doi=10.1007/978-981-10-0188-8_1 }}</ref> the study of [[viscoelastic]] materials,
in [[actuarial science]] through the [[renewal equation]],<ref>{{Cite book|last=Brunner|first=Hermann|title=Volterra Integral Equations: An Introduction to Theory and Applications|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2017|isbn=978-1107098725|series=Cambridge Monographs on Applied and Computational Mathematics|location=Cambridge, UK}}</ref> and in [[fluid mechanics]] to describe the flow behavior near finite-sized boundaries.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Daddi-Moussa-Ider|first1=A.|last2=Vilfan|first2=A.|author3-link=Ramin Golestanian|last3=Golestanian|first3=R.|title=Diffusiophoretic propulsion of an isotropic active colloidal particle near a finite-sized disk embedded in a planar fluid–fluid interface|journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics|date=6 April 2022|volume=940|pages=A12|doi=10.1017/jfm.2022.232|arxiv=2109.14437}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Daddi-Moussa-Ider|first1=A.|last2=Lisicki|first2=M.|author3-link=Hartmut Löwen|last3=Löwen|first3=H.|last4=Menzel|first4=A. M.|title=Dynamics of a microswimmer–microplatelet composite|journal=Physics of Fluids|date=5 February 2020|volume=32|issue=2|pages=021902|doi=10.1063/1.5142054|arxiv=2001.06646}}</ref>

== Conversion of Volterra equation of the first kind to the second kind ==
A linear Volterra equation of the first kind can always be reduced to a linear Volterra equation of the second kind, assuming that <math>K(t,t) \neq 0</math>.  Taking the derivative of the first kind Volterra equation gives us:<math display="block">{df\over{dt}} = \int_{a}^{t}{\partial K\over{\partial t}}x(s)ds + K(t,t)x(t)</math>Dividing through by <math>K(t,t)</math> yields:<math display="block">x(t) = {1\over{K(t,t)}}{df\over{dt}} - \int_{a}^{t}{1\over{K(t,t)}}{\partial K\over{\partial t}}x(s)ds</math>Defining <math display="inline">\widetilde{f}(t) = {1\over{K(t,t)}}{df\over{dt}}</math> and <math display="inline">\widetilde{K}(t,s) = -{1\over{K(t,t)}}{\partial K\over{\partial t}}</math> completes the transformation of the first kind equation into a linear Volterra equation of the second kind.

== Numerical solution using trapezoidal rule ==
A standard method for computing the numerical solution of a linear Volterra equation of the second kind is the [[trapezoidal rule]], which for equally-spaced subintervals <math>\Delta x</math> is given by:<math display="block">\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx \approx {\Delta x\over{2}}\left[f(x_{0}) + 2\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} f(x_{i}) + f(x_{n}) \right ]</math>Assuming equal spacing for the subintervals, the integral component of the Volterra equation may be approximated by:<math display="block">\int_{a}^{t}K(t,s)x(s)ds \approx {\Delta s\over{2}}\left[K(t,s_{0})x(s_{0}) + 2K(t,s_{1})x(s_{1}) + \cdots + 2K(t,s_{n-1})x(s_{n-1}) + K(t,s_{n})x(s_{n}) \right ]</math>Defining <math>x_{i} = x(s_{i})</math>, <math>f_{i} = f(t_{i})</math>, and <math>K_{ij} = K(t_{i},s_{j})</math>, we have the [[system of linear equations]]:<math display="block">\begin{aligned}
x_{0} &= f_{0} \\
x_{1} &= f_{1} + {\Delta s\over{2}}\left(K_{10}x_{0} + K_{11}x_{1} \right ) \\
x_{2} &= f_{2} + {\Delta s\over{2}}\left(K_{20}x_{0} + 2K_{21}x_{1} + K_{22}x_{2} \right ) \\
&\vdots \\
x_{n} &= f_{n} + {\Delta s\over{2}}\left(K_{n0}x_{0} + 2K_{n1}x_{1} + \cdots + 2K_{n,n-1}x_{n-1} + K_{nn}x_{n} \right )
\end{aligned}</math>This is equivalent to the [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] equation:<math display="block">x = f + Mx \implies x = (I-M)^{-1}f</math>For well-behaved kernels, the trapezoidal rule tends to work well.

== Application: Ruin theory ==
One area where Volterra integral equations appear is in [[ruin theory]], the study of the risk of insolvency in actuarial science. The objective is to quantify the probability of ruin <math>\psi(u) = \mathbb{P}[\tau(u) < \infty]</math>, where <math>u</math> is the initial surplus and <math>\tau(u)</math> is the time of ruin. In the [[Ruin theory#Classical model|classical model]] of ruin theory, the net cash position <math>X_{t}</math> is a function of the initial surplus, premium income earned at rate <math>c</math>, and outgoing claims <math>\xi</math>:<math display="block">X_{t} = u + ct - \sum_{i=1}^{N_{t}}\xi_{i}, \quad t \geq 0 </math>where <math>N_{t}</math> is a [[Poisson point process|Poisson process]] for the number of claims with intensity <math>\lambda</math>. Under these circumstances, the ruin probability may be represented by a Volterra integral equation of the form<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kent.ac.uk/smsas/personal/lb209/files/risk-notes-10.pdf|title=Lecture Notes on Risk Theory|date=February 20, 2010|website=School of Mathematics, Statistics and Actuarial Science|publisher=University of Kent|pages=17-22}}</ref>:<math display="block">\psi(u) = {\lambda\over{c}}\int_{u}^{\infty}S(x)dx + {\lambda\over{c}}\int_{0}^{u}\psi(u-x)S(x)dx </math>where <math>S(\cdot)</math> is the [[survival function]] of the claims distribution.

== Stochastic Volterra Equation ==
We say that the process <math>X_t</math> is solution to a stochastic Volterra
<ref>{{cite web |last= Abi Jaber et altri|date=23 October 2019 |title= Affine Volterra processes|url= https://arxiv.org/pdf/1708.08796}}</ref>
equation if
<math>
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t K(t-s)b(x_s)ds + \int_0^t K(t-s) \sigma(X_s)dW_s
</math> 

where we assume <math>X_t</math> to be adapted to the filtration of a [[probability space]] with the usual conditions. One model using this framework is for example the Rough Bergomi Model.
